paragraphs: Blindly explore and compare persistent, scene-scale 3D worlds generated from the same case: a starter image and caption, or for prompt-only LLM cases a text prompt alone. A ranked entry must be a self-contained GLB mesh, Gaussian-splat PLY/SPZ, or a native NeRF bundle with a validated deterministic browser derivative. Videos, panoramas, ordinary point clouds, isolated-object assets, and non-explorable NeRFs are rejected; the exception is an LLM case that asks for an object, such as the Boeing 747, whose program must still build it at real-world scale.

The public and admin Spaces are CPU-only. Generation uses separately budgeted Hugging Face Jobs and never runs in a viewer request. During development every repository, Dataset, Bucket, PR, input, output, preview, and score is private. At release, only the public Space, release Dataset, and artifact Bucket can be made public; ballots and operational state remain private.

paragraphs: LogoLabs' Agate text-to-image models (a 0.19B flow generator with a 68M text encoder) running as a static page. The tokenizer, text encoder, 50-step flow sampler with classifier-free guidance and the TAESD decoder all run on your own GPU through WebGPU (onnxruntime-web).
Runs entirely in your browser — prompts never leave your machine. There is no server and no API call.

Why we built Agate. Agate is LogoLabs' search for the best architecture for small-scale image generation, as groundwork for glyph and symbol generation: we want to generate vector-native fonts to go with the wordmarks we make at LogoLabs. We trained a general text-to-image model because general image generation is a good proxy for how an architecture performs on those tasks, and it is very benchmark-friendly (GenEval, Qwen-Image-Bench, FID), unlike tasks such as SDF generation, which have almost no established benchmarks. Next, we plan to build on it to generate SVGs with our vectoriser,…

repositories.name: Defeating the trainer-generator precision mismatch in TRL
repositories.description: An interactive AI application on Hugging Face Spaces.

paragraphs: Phantom PPO clipping from numerical precision gaps prevents RL convergence.

We show that async GRPO training fails when the training forward pass (FP32) and the vLLM inference server (BF16) use different numerical precision. The root cause is a precision gap that triggers phantom PPO clipping, zeroing out gradient signal for tokens whose policy has not actually changed.

This repository hosts the interactive research article Defeating the trainer-generator precision mismatch in TRL, by Amine Dirhoussi, Quentin Gallouédec, Edward Beeching, Lewis Tunstall, Kashif Rasul, and Leandro von Werra (Hugging Face).
features: BF16 arithmetic and where precision loss originates
The GRPO loss and the role of the importance sampling ratio
How small logit errors amplify into large policy ratio deviations
Phantom clipping and gradient corruption in async rollouts
Interventions that restore convergence

repositories.name: Wan Loop Generator
repositories.description: An interactive AI application on Hugging Face Spaces.

paragraphs: A minimal Gradio Space that generates a seamless downloadable video loop from one image and a prompt. The output selector offers MKV (High Quality) by default and MP4 (Compressed). The prompt is passed unchanged to the text encoder. There is no autoprompt, hidden negative prompt, or filename-based preset.

Every result includes an embedded browser-compatible H.264 preview and a separate download in the selected format. MKV downloads therefore retain AV1 quality without sacrificing in-page playback; MP4 selection reuses one file for both preview and download.

The runtime uses vendored ComfyUI-WanVideoWrapper nodes with two Wan 2.2 I2V passes (high-noise and low-noise), identical start and end images, RIFE seam interpolation, resident tiled RealESRGANx2plus upscaling, and selectable AV1/MKV or H.264/MP4 encoding at 1280x720 and 17 fps. MKV uses the reference Thunar SUPERIOR preset (libsvtav1, preset 6, CRF 45); MP4 uses libx264, preset slow, CRF 28, tune film and faststart. Wan inference remains 832x480, so HD output does not increase diffusion token count.

repositories.description: SASS decoding, semantics, p-code, decompilation, emulation

paragraphs: Assemble SASS source or upload a CUDA .cubin and explore what nvdisasm-re recovers from NVIDIA's nvdisasm:

Emulation needs each architecture's launch-constant layout (known for all but SM107). nvcc's SM90+ code reaches global memory through explicit descriptors, whose semantics are still opaque, so whole kernels run on SM75-SM89.

Every architecture nvdisasm 13.4 describes is supported: SM75, SM80, SM86, SM89, SM90, SM100, SM101, SM103, SM107 and SM120 (SM87/SM88, SM110 and SM121 cubins decode as SM86, SM101 and SM120, as in nvdisasm).
features: Disassembly: the pure-Python decoder (pydecode), which matches nvdisasm's text, with the machine-description class each word matched.
Lifted IR: Ghidra-free instruction semantics as register writes, stores and control flow.
P-code: Ghidra's p-code per instruction from the generated SLEIGH languages (SM75–SM120, exact or readable floating point).
High p-code and Decompiled C: Ghidra's decompiler on the whole kernel, as its simplified SSA p-code per basic block and as C.
Emulate: run a kernel in Ghidra's p-code emulator and, per thread, in the Python evaluator, and compare the traces step by step.

repositories.name: SMILES Subword Vocabularies
repositories.description: How BPE and Unigram-LM carve up chemistry SMILES differently

paragraphs: An interactive companion to "Where to cut, how deep: BPE and Unigram-LM on chemistry SMILES" (arXiv:2607.05691).

Pick a molecule and see both tokenizers segment it, aligned on the shared glyph stream. It surfaces the paper's three contrasts live: membership (near-disjoint vocabularies, small Jaccard), granularity (Unigram-LM stays near-atomic and emits more tokens; BPE packs more glyphs per token), and compatibility (they agree on where to cut but differ in how deeply, so BPE's parse is usually a strict coarsening of Unigram-LM's).

Runs entirely in your browser via Pyodide: a static page, no server, no cost. The tokenizer logic is a pure-Python reimplementation (segmenter.py) validated byte-for-byte against smirk; the shipped tokenizers/ bundle holds only each cell's tokenizer.json + meta.yaml.

whatItDoes.text: An interactive companion to "Where to cut, how deep: BPE and Unigram-LM on chemistry SMILES" (arXiv:2607.05691).
